title: I cut Grok and Gemini from my AI stock-research panel. Here's how they screwed the pooch.
author: Frodo_Baghodler
selftext:
One paper-trading build, so treat this as a case study. All four models worked in the same shared conversation with the same search tools, on unequal jobs. It shows what happened in my workflow. YMMV. The original setup: A script screened \~680 US stocks to 42 momentum names. Grok went first (why is each stock up, is it crowded, strongest fact against it, pick 8), Gemini fact-checked all 42 against filings, Claude ran risk, and GPT-6 Astra audited all of it.

**What Grok got wrong:**

   \- Said PANW "didn't spike" in the AI-security rally. Its own table showed +11% in five days; PANW was +13.1% that Monday.

   \- Called an FDA date 85 days away "inside a 10-week hold."

Ranked ETON and NESR in its top 8 while both closed below their 20-day average, which breaks a hard entry rule.

   \- Called ABCL's 1 Oct conference talk a "binary event"; the data had been released 10 Aug.

It also found six pending buyouts hiding in a momentum list, which was helpful, but inside my agent it used the same web search as everyone else, with no native X feed, so the "crowding" role never added data the others lacked.

**What Gemini got wrong:**

   \- "Quoted" NTAP's FY27 guide as $7.85–8.05B revenue / $9.50–9.70 EPS. The 8-K says $7.975–8.225B / $9.73–10.03.

   \- Wrote "None" in the dilution column for names it hadn't searched. Missed: TWST's $300M priced offering, ABCL's \~$200M raise, CMPS's at-the-market share sales.

   \- It pinned Grok's errors on another model and cited "rule 16" of a six-rule document (Bruh...). It did correctly separate FA's sponsor block sale from company dilution.

Why cut instead of fix:  Every extra round added review time and new errors to check, and the reviews weren't catching what a full redo caught. The two I kept sometimes miss things too: Claude confirmed CMPS's wrong "no dilution" claim in September. Last week Claude's draft trade plan had the wrong pre-earnings exit date and an arithmetic error. Astra caught both. Astra then caught a false "always lower risk" claim in Claude's revision. Astra's been the highest performer of the 4 thus far, and it's not even close. It eats tokens like crazy tho, unfortunately, so I'm continuing to tune the model choice and thinking level for the various tasks.

New rule: Astra and Claude each do the entire job (screen, sources, sizing) and save it before reading the other's. Both must approve the identical plan; either can block. Grok or Gemini can still answer a narrow question when there's a reason to ask. Since the switch, the pair has cleared only one position: HNGE, after four plan revisions. It's doing well since I entered the position on 10/7.

comments.author: leroylabs
comments.body: Having Astra and Claude save independent plans is a good control, but identical approval can still hide correlated errors if both search the same sources. I’d turn the failures into a fixed regression set: the NTAP FY27 figures from the 8-K, ETON/NESR versus the 20-day average, the ABCL event date, and each missed dilution. Score citation support, rule compliance, arithmetic, and abstention separately before changing model or thinking level. Also keep every rejected HNGE revision, since whether later passes corrected old errors or introduced new ones is more informative than the final agreement.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: the None in the dilution column for names it never searched is the worst one there, an empty cell that looks like an answer. I'd make 'not checked' its own value. judging which model was right also needs the 8 picks to run forward, and Quantradin does that part, I built it so an AI can hand over picks and have them tracked on real prices with pretend money. quantradin.com

comments.author: Frodo_Baghodler
comments.body: Somebody said it seems like a lot of hand holding and asked what my time driver is now but deleted their comment. In case anyone else has the same question, it IS a lot of hand holding and that's one reason I'm dropping the "problem children." Right now the time sink is full refreshes from Astra. Maybe it says more about my laptop than the process but it takes an hour or more.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Having each model do the whole job and save it before reading the other's is the right fix, and the examples are easy to check because each one has a number you can look up. The thing I'd add is a plain scorecard: count every factual claim a model made that could be checked against a filing, and how many were wrong, by model and by type of claim (dates, numbers, dilution). With only one position cleared so far, the P&L can't separate the models, so the error counts are the evidence. Dates like earnings, FDA decisions and offerings are exactly where models slip, and Cymetica's Event Cards are one place to look at event markets built around scheduled dates.
